title: Browser Security
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terminology of Browser Security.
Apply browser security to a small synthetic example and identify evidence that supports the conclusion.
Identify a relevant limitation or failure mode and describe a safe defensive response.

content.intro: This lesson covers browser security in the Web Application Security track. It preserves the PDF's listed subtopics and develops a small, checkable defensive example. You will practice stating scope and assumptions, selecting relevant evidence, and describing what remains uncertain.
content.why_it_matters: Validate on the server, encode output for its context, use parameterized database access, and enforce access checks on every protected operation. The specific focus here is browser security; connect each subtopic to an observable check or a documented decision.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Browser Security focuses on browser security model; cookies and storage; same-origin policy and cross-origin controls. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case.

items.title: Browser Security Model
items.text: AI-enabled applications add risks around untrusted inputs, data exposure, model and dependency provenance, tool permissions, evaluation, and over-trusting generated output. Keep retrieval and tool actions constrained, minimize sensitive data, and use human review for high-impact decisions.

items.title: Cookies and Storage
items.text: API and identity protections must validate protocol details, token issuer/audience/expiry, resource-level permissions, and request limits on the server. Browser CORS policy is not a replacement for authentication or authorization.

items.title: Same-Origin Policy and Cross-Origin Controls
items.text: Treat user-controlled input as untrusted across every parser and output context. Use parameterized queries, context-aware output encoding, strict server-side authorization, safe resource allowlists, and regression tests; validate only in a controlled local application.

items.title: Content Security Policy
items.text: Treat user-controlled input as untrusted across every parser and output context. Use parameterized queries, context-aware output encoding, strict server-side authorization, safe resource allowlists, and regression tests; validate only in a controlled local application.

items.title: Subresource Integrity
items.text: Integrity means data and system state remain accurate and protected against unauthorized or accidental change. Identify trusted sources, validation checks, and evidence that a change was expected.

items.title: Clickjacking and Frame Restrictions
items.text: Treat user-controlled input as untrusted across every parser and output context. Use parameterized queries, context-aware output encoding, strict server-side authorization, safe resource allowlists, and regression tests; validate only in a controlled local application.

items.title: Browser Privacy and Tracking Risks
items.text: Privacy engineering limits collection and use to a defined purpose, restricts access, controls retention and deletion, and prepares for rights requests and incidents. Jurisdictional obligations require an applicability check against current official materials.

content_blocks.title: Defensive example (synthetic data)
content_blocks.code:
import sqlite3

# In-memory database; user data is never sent anywhere.
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE demo_users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO demo_users(email) VALUES (?)", ("learner@example.test",))
email = "learner@example.test"
row = db.execute("SELECT id FROM demo_users WHERE email = ?", (email,)).fetchone()
print("matched demo user:", row[0])
db.close()
content_blocks.notes: This example uses synthetic values and has no network dependency. CodeLeaf displays it as instructional text; production does not execute arbitrary learner code.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification
content_blocks.text: Web application security is about enforcing trust boundaries in browsers, servers, databases, and user-controlled data flows. Before attempting any live security test, obtain explicit permission and verify that the target and method are within scope. When a secure isolated runner is not available, treat the code as a local/synthetic example and do not run arbitrary content on production infrastructure.

content_blocks.title: Run, verify, and reset
content_blocks.text: Review the python snippet as a local calculation. If you choose to run this example, use Python 3 and synthetic inputs in a disposable local environment; compare the displayed expected output with what you observe. If the result differs, check the copied inputs and runtime version, restore the synthetic input, and repeat. No scan, external request, or production change is needed.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Browser Security focuses on browser security model; cookies and storage; same-origin policy and cross-origin controls. Define the system or data in scope, the expected behavior, and the consequences if that behavior fails. Then select a proportionate control and identify evidence that can verify both the normal path and an important failure case. Apply this to one controlled example, record evidence, and note an important edge case. Next, continue to the next lesson or revisit the prerequisite concept if a key term is unclear.

content.task: Create a concise, reviewable artifact demonstrating Browser Security. Use synthetic data or a controlled local training environment only. Include the relevant syllabus subtopics (Browser Security Model; Cookies and Storage; Same-Origin Policy and Cross-Origin Controls), state assumptions, show what evidence would support your conclusion, identify one failure mode, and recommend a defensive next step. Do not test systems outside written authorization.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use only a synthetic dataset, a disposable local lab, or an explicitly authorized system.
Include a clear scope/assumption statement and enough sanitized evidence for another learner to follow the reasoning.
Explain one limitation, edge case, or failure mode.
Recommend a proportionate defensive control and describe how to verify it safely.
hints: Write the expected behavior and test boundary before looking at a result.
Change one assumption at a time; compare results against the original synthetic case.
Record evidence and uncertainty separately, and select a proportionate protective action.
troubleshooting: The example is illustrative and should be reviewed against current platform/version documentation before production use.
If an output differs, check the input and runtime version; do not broaden the activity to an unrelated system.
Use only fake data and remove all temporary local artifacts when the exercise is complete.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one observation as conclusive proof.
common_mistakes.why: Security telemetry and tests cover only the cases they were designed to observe.
common_mistakes.fix: Corroborate important claims and document coverage gaps.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing a target without confirming authorization.
common_mistakes.why: A technical ability to reach a system does not grant permission to assess it.
common_mistakes.fix: Use synthetic input or a local lab; stop if the approved scope is unclear.

common_mistakes.problem: Skipping the version and context assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Security controls and protocol details vary across implementations and deployment models.
common_mistakes.fix: Record versions, configuration, expected output, and the source used for verification.

summary: Browser Security is best understood within its defined scope and trust boundaries.
Use relevant evidence and test both an expected case and a meaningful failure case.
Record uncertainty and choose a proportionate, authorized defensive next step.
